content: Plastic bags are a practical and hygienic solution for managing waste and are widely utilized for this purpose. These bags are lightweight and particularly effective for containing messy or wet waste, such as food scraps, as they help to minimize odors. They are also commonly used to line waste bins or containers, ensuring that the container itself remains clean by preventing direct contact with the waste. Once the bag is full, it can be easily removed by pulling its edges, sealed, and tied with minimal contact with the waste material. Plastic garbage bags are available in various sizes and are typically sold in packets or rolls containing several dozen bags. Some bags come with wire twist ties for secure closure, while others feature drawstrings, handles, or perforations for easier handling and sealing. The most commonly used material for manufacturing these bags is low-density polyethylene (LDPE), which is soft and flexible. For added strength, linear low-density polyethylene (LLDPE) is often used, and in some cases, high-density polyethylene (HDPE) is employed. The invention of the plastic garbage bag dates back to 1950 and is credited to Canadians Harry Wasylyk, Larry Hansen, and Frank Plomp. In a CBC television special, the green garbage bag was ranked 36th among the top 50 Canadian inventions. Plastic bags can be incinerated along with their contents in waste-to-energy facilities, and they remain stable and inert in sanitary landfills. Some plastic bags are made from biodegradable polyethylene film, which decomposes when exposed to air, sunlight, and moisture or when subjected to composting. However, these bags do not readily decompose in sealed landfill environments and may pose a contamination risk to plastic recycling processes. Oxo-biodegradable and other degradable plastic bags have specific applications, particularly as garbage bags. Organic waste can be placed in oxo-biodegradable plastic sacks and sent directly to composting facilities without opening the bags, reducing odors, disease transmission by insects, and handling risks. The resulting compost can be utilized by farmers and growers. Oxo-biodegradable plastic, unlike starch-based alternatives, releases carbon slowly, producing high-quality compost. While it does not degrade quickly in low-temperature windrow composting, it is suitable for in-vessel composting at the higher temperatures required by modern animal by-products regulations. Oxo-biodegradable plastics undergo a process of peroxidation and embrittlement, behaving like natural waste. They are bio-assimilated by bacteria and fungi, which convert the degraded plastic into cell biomass, similar to lignocellulosic materials. This type of plastic is engineered to fragment through a combination of photo-oxidation and thermo-oxidation, allowing it to degrade even in the absence of light.
